content: Rubella, also known as German measles or 3-day measles, is a common childhood infection that typically causes minimal systemic disturbance. However, transient arthropathy may occur in adults. Serious complications are exceedingly rare. If not for the potential effects of transplacental infection on a developing fetus, rubella would be considered a relatively mild infection. The clinical presentation of rubella was first described in 1814, and its association with congenital anomalies was identified in 1942. The rubella virus was first isolated in 1962 by two independent research groups using tissue culture techniques. The pathophysiology of rubella is not fully understood. After transmission via contact with respiratory droplets from an infected individual, the virus replicates in the respiratory epithelium. This is followed by viremia, which peaks at the time the characteristic rubella rash appears. Rubella is caused by the rubella virus, an enveloped togavirus with a single-stranded RNA genome. The virus is transmitted through the respiratory route and replicates in the nasopharynx and lymph nodes. It can be detected in the bloodstream 5 to 7 days after infection and subsequently spreads throughout the body. Importantly, the virus is capable of crossing the placenta and infecting the fetus. Rubella must be differentiated from other diseases that present with skin rash, fever, and lymphadenopathy, such as measles, coxsackievirus infection, and infectious mononucleosis. In the United States, endemic transmission of the rubella virus has been eliminated since 2001. Between 2004 and 2013, only 10 cases of rubella infection were diagnosed, all in immigrants. Risk factors for rubella infection include contact with an infected individual and lack of immunization according to standard vaccination schedules. There are no standard screening tests recommended for rubella infection. However, pregnant women with suspected rubella infection must undergo diagnostic testing to confirm the infection and prevent fetal anomalies. Rubella is transmitted through direct contact and typically presents with fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy. It is usually a self-limiting infection that resolves without complications. In rare cases, complications such as arthritis may occur, which require symptomatic treatment. The prognosis in adults is generally favorable, with complete resolution of symptoms within a week. Patients with rubella infection commonly present with fever, a skin rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Symptoms such as malaise and anorexia often precede the onset of fever and rash. On physical examination, adults with rubella infection may exhibit low-grade fever and a maculopapular rash that begins on the face and spreads caudally. Cervical lymphadenopathy is present in the majority of cases. All patients with suspected rubella infection should undergo further investigation to confirm the diagnosis. Serological tests to detect rubella-specific IgG antibodies and IgG avidity, as well as reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), are recommended for diagnostic confirmation. There is no specific antiviral therapy for rubella infection. Management is primarily symptomatic, and cases should be reported to local disease control agencies. Surgical intervention is not indicated for the management of rubella. Rubella infections can be prevented through active immunization programs using live attenuated virus vaccines. Two effective live attenuated vaccines, the RA 27/3 and Cendehill strains, are available for the prevention of adult disease. All patients with confirmed rubella infection should be vaccinated. Pregnant women should receive vaccination after delivery to prevent future infections.
